title: How to check if someone is who they say they are
summary: How to check if someone is who they say they are: test whether their name, photo, phone and email lead to one real person. Sixtyfour runs the research.
body_markdown:
Write down every detail they have given you, then check that the name, photo, phone number and email address all lead to the same person, that the person appears on pages they do not control, and that their history online is as old as their story. Look for the same details under another name, and confirm anything important through a channel you found yourself. Stop if they ask for money or documents before you have met.


From outside a platform you can check that the details you were given describe one real person: reverse search their photos, look up their phone number and email address, and look for them on pages other people wrote, such as an employer's team page. Checking an identity document properly means examining the document and matching it to a live face, which identity verification services and platforms' own sign-up checks do. A photo of an ID sent in a message is only a picture, and the FBI warns that criminals generate fake ones.


It tells you where a photo has appeared before. If it appears on older pages under another name, the profile is very likely using someone else's photo, which the FTC calls a sign of a scam. A match under the same name shows only that the photo belongs to that person, and no match settles nothing, because a private person's photo and an AI-generated face can both leave no trace.


A live video call is good evidence that a person looks like their photos, and it falls short of proof. The FBI warns that criminals use generated video in real time video chats and to make an online contact seem to be a real person, and suggests looking for imperfections such as lag and unrealistic movements. Confirm the identity through a channel you found yourself as well, such as a call to the employer's main number.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes the name, email address, phone number and profile links someone has given you, finds who each detail leads to and whether the person appears on pages other than their own, and returns each researched field with its sources and, when you turn on confidence scoring, a score for each field. It does not examine identity documents or verify selfies. A field it could not establish comes back empty, and you decide what to do.


Stop replying, and send no money, documents or personal details. Report the account to the platform where you met, and report the scam to the FTC and to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center. If you paid, contact your bank or the company you used to pay right away, tell them you paid a scammer and ask them to refund your money.
